title: John Cage
content_html:
John Cage

John Cage’s use of the I Ching (Yijing) is one of the most famous modern applications of the book outside of divination. He turned it into a tool for artistic composition, embedding Taoist and chance principles into Western avant-garde music. Cage used the I Ching as a random number generator, by casting coins (or later consulting computer simulations of the oracle), he mapped the 64 hexagrams to musical decisions (pitches, durations, dynamics, timbres and order of musical fragments). This allowed him to remove personal preference and ego from composition, allowing music to arise from processes of nature and chance, not from personal intention.

Cage often emphasized that he was not interested in expressing himself, but in letting sounds be themselves. He used the I Ching to bypass taste and habit, creating a music of openness, indeterminacy, and relational meaning. In this sense, he extended the I Ching’s role as a book of change into an aesthetic practice of change itself.

After the 1960s he increasingly applied I Ching-based chance operations to drawing, printmaking, and even writing. He collaborated with print workshops (notably Crown Point Press in San Francisco) from the 1970s onward. He used I Ching coin tosses to determine placement of lines or marks on a page, thickness of lines, types of paper, colors, or inks, and layering or sequence of stencils/etchings Works like Where R = Ryoanji (1983–92) involved tracing stones with chance-determined positions and repetitions, echoing Zen gardens.
